title: The Impact of Markovian Errors on Random Circuits
authors: Anthony M. Polloreno, Timothy Proctor, Robin Blume-Kohout
abstract: Randomized benchmarking (RB) returns a single decay parameter or gate error rate, but when the noise is gate-dependent that parameter is notoriously difficult to interpret. We study RB and related random-circuit benchmarks under small gate-local Markovian noise by factorizing each noisy gate into its ideal action followed by the exponential of a small error generator and then perturbing the RB $\mathscr{L}$ matrix, which models the RB decay. For any low-error gate set that satisfies the requirements of RB (it is a sequence-asymptotic unitary 2-design), we show that Pauli-stochastic error rates contribute linearly to the RB decay parameter, while Hamiltonian error rates contribute through a gauge-invariant quadratic form. Pauli-correlation and active generators are absent from the linear term and enter only at higher order. For the single-qubit native gate set $\{X_{π/2},Y_{π/2}\}$ we derive this quadratic form explicitly in terms of three first-order gauge-invariant (FOGI) coordinates: the two intrinsic over-rotations and one relational axis-tilt error. The resulting formula explains the dependence of DRB on the sampling distribution and the compilation dependence of CRB. These results turn RB decay rates into interpretable functions of experimentally meaningful elementary error rates.
summary: This paper develops a theoretical framework to correctly interpret the error rate measured by Randomized Benchmarking (RB) when noise is complex and gate-dependent. By modeling noise using small Markovian generators, the authors show that the error rate decomposes into distinct, physically meaningful contributions (linear from Pauli noise, quadratic from Hamiltonian noise). This allows experimentalists to extract elementary error parameters from a single measured decay rate.
main_problem: The primary challenge is interpreting the error rate measured by Randomized Benchmarking (RB) when the underlying noise is gate-dependent, as the naive average infidelity fails to capture the true error structure.
main_result: The analysis shows that Pauli-stochastic errors contribute linearly to the RB decay parameter, while Hamiltonian errors contribute through a gauge-invariant quadratic form. These results allow RB decay rates to be expressed as interpretable functions of elementary error rates.
method: The authors perturb the RB decay matrix by modeling noisy gates using small, gate-local Markovian error generators and employing First-Order Gauge-Invariant (FOGI) coordinates to maintain physical interpretability.
model_or_system: The study analyzes quantum processors characterized by specific gate sets (e.g., $\{X\pi/2, Y\pi/2\}$) subjected to small, gate-local Markovian noise, modeled via Lindbladian error generators.
key_observables: The RB decay parameter ($r$), the quadratic form $Q^{(2)}_{	ext{CRB}}$, and the error rate $D_{	ext{CRB}}$.
important_parameters: The small error regime (perturbative expansion), the sampling distribution parameters ($\Omega_X$), and the structure of the error generators (Hamiltonian, Pauli-stochastic, etc.).
main_assumptions: The analysis is restricted to the perturbative regime of small gate-local Markovian noise, and the error process is assumed to be Markovian.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate how the measured RB error rates depend non-trivially on the sampling distribution and the specific error model, showing deviations from simple weighted-infidelity heuristics.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theory by first analyzing the structure of the error generators, deriving the linear and quadratic contributions to the decay parameter, and finally applying this framework to specific gate sets to derive explicit, gauge-invariant error formulas.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous theoretical framework for interpreting experimental quantum characterization tools like RB, linking abstract decay parameters to physically measurable, gauge-invariant error components relevant for designing fault-tolerant quantum computation.
